title: Trump FCC faces blowback in attempt to police speech on broadcast TV

Conservatives and liberals lined up in opposition to the Federal Communications Commission’s attempt to punish ABC for speech that President Trump dislikes.
Liberal advocacy groups urged FCC Chairman Brendan Carr to end his attacks on ABC, and conservative groups warned Carr not to set a precedent that would harm conservatives in future administrations. Former FCC chairs and commissioners from prior Republican and Democratic administrations also joined in opposition to what they call Carr’s “campaign to censor disfavored speech and advance the president’s personal interest.”
The FCC recently ordered ABC to file early license-renewal applications for the eight TV stations it owns and operates. A petition to deny ABC’s license renewals was then submitted by the Center for American Rights, a conservative group whose previous petitions factored heavily into Carr’s “news distortion” investigations into broadcasters accused of bias against Republicans and Trump. Another petition to deny was filed by the conservative Media Research Center.
There was a July 29 deadline for people to submit oppositions to the petitions to deny ABC’s license renewals, and there is an August 5 deadline for replies to the opposition filings.
“Through this proceeding, the FCC seeks to censor Disney’s and ABC’s speech and send a chilling message to all broadcasters: carry speech we don’t like at your peril,” said a filing submitted by former Republican and Democratic FCC chairs and commissioners from the Reagan, George H.W. Bush, Clinton, and Obama eras.

Ars VideoHow Lighting Design In The Callisto Protocol Elevates The HorrorAlthough the Trump FCC says the proceeding is over ABC’s potential violation of anti-discrimination rules with diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) practices, it was statements by Jimmy Kimmel that seemed to spur Carr into action on Trump’s behalf. In September 2025, Carr threatened to revoke ABC station licenses for “news distortion” if they continued airing Kimmel’s show. In April of this year, Carr ordered the highly unusual ABC license review one day after Trump and the first lady called for Kimmel to be fired over a joke in which he said Melania Trump looked like an “expectant widow.”

Conservative groups warn FCC
Despite two conservative groups petitioning the FCC to deny ABC’s license renewals, some conservative groups say the agency should not police speech and that the proceeding could set a precedent that would harm conservatives in future administrations.
“We take no position on the merits of any particular application before the Commission in any pending matter,” said a filing by 14 conservative and free-market groups, including the Center for Individual Freedom, American Commitment, and Grover Norquist’s Americans for Tax Reform. “Our concern is that establishing precedents of non-routine renewal creates a powerful lever that future FCCs—including ones hostile to conservative, religious, or otherwise disfavored broadcasters—would be all too willing to pull. The surest protection against that future is to keep the renewal process predictable today.”
The FCC historically reserved non-routine license renewals “for genuinely extraordinary circumstances, such as failures that go to a station’s basic capacity to maintain its operation or malfeasance,” the filing said, pointing to cases in which a station held an on-air contest that contributed to a listener’s death and a station that went dark for extended periods. “Preserving that high and content-neutral bar is precisely what keeps the Commission out of the business of judging speech,” the filing said.
The American Civil Liberties Union, Knight First Amendment Institute, and other free speech groups told the FCC that it has abused its regulatory power to violate the First Amendment right to free speech. They wrote that “the actions and statements by Chairman Carr and President Trump leading up to the Order demonstrate that the agency’s genuine motivation is to pressure Disney to censor viewpoints that Chairman Carr, and the president, do not like.”

Dozens of Democratic members of Congress submitted filings supporting ABC and criticizing the FCC. It doesn’t appear that any Republican lawmakers did the same, though Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) recently teamed up with Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) on legislation designed to rein in federal officials who try to coerce broadcasters or tech platforms into restricting speech. Cruz and Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) criticized Carr’s attacks on ABC during last year’s fight over Kimmel’s show.

Disney says it broke no rules
The FCC docket has received over 153,000 comments, mostly coming from individuals.
“When given the chance to weigh in on whether to allow the FCC to continue its campaign of censorship and control, the American public showed up in a big way, and the vast majority who spoke up delivered the same message,” Anna Gomez, the only Democratic commissioner on the FCC, said today. “They believe in the value of their local news, they trust those who cover their communities, and they understand that the FCC has no business deciding who is a journalist and what counts as real news. A small number of partisan voices tried to hijack this process into a referendum on a network they dislike, but the public refuses to let local stations become collateral damage in the FCC’s political games.”
Carr has multiple proceedings open against ABC, including one questioning whether The View should continue to be exempt from the equal-time rule as a “bona fide news interview program.” ABC urged viewers to write to the FCC, saying “the FCC wants to control who is allowed on the show.” The FCC responded by accusing ABC owner Disney of “a campaign of misinformation” and of “misleading viewers about the law.”

Although a July 5 Semafor report said The View is “proceeding cautiously with political candidate bookings while the FCC’s equal-time inquiry” unfolds, Disney is fighting the FCC proceedings. Disney and the ABC stations it owns yesterday filed their opposition to the petitions to deny the license renewals. Similar to its previous filings, Disney said the Trump administration is retaliating against ABC for exercising its First Amendment rights.
“For years, President Trump has expressly demanded that the Commission revoke ABC’s broadcast licenses for speech he dislikes. Since his appointment, Chairman Carr has subsequently opened all manner of investigations and issued a slew of burdensome investigatory requests,” Disney said.
Disney said ABC-owned stations have not violated the FCC’s news distortion policy, the broadcast hoax rule, the equal-time rule, or the discrimination rules the FCC cited in opening the proceeding.
“Calling up the license of a single Station—let alone all eight at once—while the Commission’s DEI investigation has found no violation is unnecessary, premature, and punitive,” Disney said. “Even if any violation were ever substantiated, the Commission has a graduated set of well-established remedies far short of the corporate death penalty of license non-renewal.”
ABC angered Trump again by not airing speech
On July 16, with the license proceeding ongoing, ABC and NBC decided not to air a Trump primetime address, though they did stream the speech online and report on the speech in breaking news segments. Trump responded with another call to revoke ABC and NBC licenses. The Center for American Rights told Carr that the failure to air the speech should be held against ABC in the license proceeding.

“The following week, Chairman Carr commented at a public press conference that the President’s speech was ‘something that broadcasters should be carrying,’ and suggested that the network’s decision not to broadcast the President’s speech would be raised and considered by the Commission during these license renewal proceedings,” Disney said.
Carr has been cagey on the potential outcome of the license renewal proceeding. “We’re going to follow the facts and the law wherever it goes,” he has said.
Legal experts say it’s unlikely that the FCC could revoke ABC licenses. A 1996 change to US telecommunications law made it nearly impossible to deny a renewal. Ordering a station to file early renewal applications also doesn’t change the actual dates the current licenses expire. The eight ABC stations are scheduled for renewals between 2028 and 2031.
Even if ABC beats the attempts to take away its licenses, Carr may succeed in chilling the speech of broadcasters. “Faced with such danger, any broadcaster would question whether its speech is worth the cost,” Disney told the FCC yesterday. “Indeed, the public record is replete with examples of other broadcasters who, when faced with similar pressures, quickly folded to the administration’s demands.”
Disney’s filing pointed to Paramount’s merger approval after it reached a $16 million settlement with Trump, canceled Stephen Colbert’s show, and “created an ombudsman to field complaints of ideological bias.” Disney further noted that various companies, including Paramount, dismantled diversity programs in exchange for FCC approval of mergers.
Disney said it has scaled back its own diversity programs during the Trump administration, but added that the FCC “has made no indication here that some form of resolution with Disney would be possible, further underscoring that its investigation is fueled by retaliation rather than policy objectives.”
